subs.text: Hi! Let's take a quick tour of Brakeza3D: a C++ engine with OpenGL deferred rendering, scripted in Lua.
This first demo is tiny: one Lua script prints a message, the run time and the FPS, every single frame.
Input is polled from Lua. Keys I hold show up on the panel: 'held' versus 'just pressed' are different calls.
Space and E are single presses: they only fire on the first frame.
The mouse works the same way: position, buttons, and clicks.
This cube has an object script attached. 'this' is the object itself, so the same script works on anything.
Up and down along the world axes...
...forward and back along the cube's own axis...
...and rotating on the spot. Speeds are in units per second, rotations in degrees.
Rotation is just a matrix: W/S pitch, A/D yaw, Q/E roll. Each key multiplies the object's M3 by a small rotation.
Space switches on auto-rotation, applied every frame with the delta time so it's frame-rate independent.
And R puts everything back to the starting rotation.
Objects can be created from a script. Every press of C drops a random coloured point light into the scene.
V hides and shows the last one. A disabled object costs nothing.
And X removes them for good. Removed objects are cleaned up by the engine.
Parenting: four coloured lights are children of the cube. Wherever the parent goes, they follow.
Children keep their offset relative to the parent, so we can animate their orbits on top of the movement.
Switch it off and they sit still again.
The cone looks at the sphere with LookAt. Here it turns smoothly; I'm speeding that up and slowing it down.
Follow off: now I turn it by hand with A and D.
And Tab changes which object it tracks.
A follow camera is a few lines: each frame it eases towards a point behind the cube, then looks at it.
The script turns the keyboard off for the camera, so the keys only move the cube.
Scripts can talk to each other. The cube owns two variables, declared in its JSON file...
...and the sphere reads them every second through getLocalScriptVar. The values go to the console.
Lights from code. Q and E rotate the sun: the shading and the shadows follow in real time.
Z and X change the ambient light, the 'floor' of the lighting.
And a point light I created in the script, with attenuation, moves around the cubes.
Physics is Bullet. This box is a rigid body with mass and friction; W A S D push it with forces.
Space gives it an impulse: a jump.
I and K set its velocity directly instead. Different tools for different feels.
X stops all motion dead, and then... jump again.
The player box falls onto the enemy and gets knocked back: that's a collision callback running in Lua.
R fires a visible ray at the target (green is a hit), and G checks the ground below.
Skeletal animation. The yellow lines are the skeleton: every bone moves the part of the mesh attached to it.
Walk: press 2 and the character switches to the walking clip.
Run: press 3. Same bones, a different clip.
Idle: back to the standing pose.
Jump: press 4. The clip plays once, and when it ends the script sends the character back to idle.
Another jump. Watch the legs bend and the whole skeleton lift.
And one more. isAnimationEnds() tells the script when the clip is over.
B hides the skeleton...
...and shows it again.
Crouch walk is the fifth clip. Speed (P / O) and looping (L) can change while it plays.
The editor has its own debug tools. Interface, Draw Animation Bones: the skeleton goes off...
...and on again. Any animated mesh, in any scene, with no script at all.
Animations can be chosen without any script, too. Select the character in the view...
...and open Mesh3D Animation in its inspector: every clip stored in the FBX is in a list.
Click Walking and it plays at once...
...click Running and it changes again.
The Speed field sets the playback rate. Slow motion...
...and back to normal speed.
And Crouch walking, from the same list.
A particle emitter created entirely from code: fire, smoke, magic sparks and snow are just parameter sets.
Emission rate, lifetime, gravity, speed and a colour gradient. Up to 512 particles per emitter.
Space toggles the emission.
Audio from Lua: register short sounds once, then play them by name whenever you need them.
Music loops in the background, and the volume can be set live.
A scene shader, written in GLSL, tints the whole screen.
The script writes new values into the shader's variables every frame. That's how you animate effects.
Hi! A quick tour of Brakeza3D: a C++ engine with OpenGL deferred rendering, scripted in Lua.
Geometry goes into a G-Buffer first, and the lighting comes after.
Per-pixel lights, shadows and a post-process on top.
Now the editor. First, the project panel.
Project scenes: every scene the project can load. This whole tour is one project of 35 scenes.
Project scripts: global scripts that run in every scene, like this demo browser.
And the project settings: name, file, gravity and resolution.
Layouts rearrange the editor: this one, Design, gives the scene all the room.
Script Controls, Stop: with the scripts stopped, the scene becomes editable, with its grid and gizmos.
Click an object and it gets a green outline.
Pick the Move tool and drag an arrow of the gizmo: the pawn slides up along that axis.
Select another one, switch to Rotate...
...and turn it with the rotation ring.
Back in the Default layout, Object Properties is docked on the left: the inspector of the selected cube.
Transformations: position, rotation and scale.
Drag a field and the value changes live, right in the scene.
Render settings: alpha, selectable, lighting and raster state...
...down to face culling and the rest of the flags.
Attached objects: the children hanging from this one.
Collider: the physics body of the object and its mode.
Misc: the object's id, its picking colour and its distance to the camera.
Mesh3D: everything about the model.
Mesh render options: pipeline, culling, mipmaps and emission...
...scroll for the rest.
Mesh information: the model file, its submeshes and materials.
Script Controls, Play: the scripts run again.
And on with the tour.
A global directional light turns in a 30-second loop to fake day and night.
Back in the editor: the object browser groups the scene by type, lights included.
Select a spotlight and the editor draws its debug cone: the volume of space it lights.
Select something else and it goes away.
Back to the demo.
Keys 1, 2 and 3 switch the lights off and on from Lua: setEnabled on each one.
The editor's light checkboxes call exactly the same thing.
Eight full-screen shaders in a chain: the image is handed from one to the next through two ping-pong buffers.
Here's the engine's own editor. Under 'Scene Shaders' you can see all eight of them.
Each green dot is the shader's on/off switch. Turn one off and its quarter of the screen goes back to normal.
Another one... they're independent, so you can mix them freely.
And back on. This is how you'd debug a long effects chain: switch things off one by one.
This demo is the heaviest on post-processing, so it's the perfect excuse to open the profiler: Windows, Profiler.
The overview: frame time, memory, and the cost of every engine component each frame.
The Render tab breaks the frame into its passes: scripts, G-Buffer, shadows, lights, transparencies, post-processing.
Switch on GPU timing and every pass also shows the time the graphics card spent on it.
Watch the Post-Processing row while I turn all eight shaders off...
...and on again. Each shader in the chain adds a fullscreen pass.
The Render tab has more: Frame Buffers...
Every offscreen target the engine renders to, as live thumbnails.
The layers of the final image: global, scene, background, foreground and the UI.
The G-Buffer of the deferred renderer: positions, normals, albedo and depth.
And the picking buffer: a colour ID per object, how a click knows what it hit.
Post-Processing Chain: for every shader, the texture it reads and the one it writes.
That's the ping-pong: each effect feeds the next, and the last one is copied to the global buffer.
OpenGL Status: the limits of this GPU and driver...
...and the vendor, the renderer and the exact GL version in use.
Scripts: per-script timing is off by default, so measuring costs nothing until you ask for it.
Switched on, it lists how long each Lua script takes every frame. That's how the slow ones get found.
Resources: the thread pools that load assets in the background, with their queues and workloads.
Physics: how many Bullet bodies there are by type, their collision groups, and a switch for the debug wireframe.
And back to the overview. Everything here can be turned off with --no-profiler when you don't need it.
One more thing: stop the scripts, and the editor camera is free.
Zoom in on the pawn: every quarter has its own effect.
And out: the whole scene is filtered, not just the pawn.
Play again, and on with the tour.
Node shaders: fourteen objects, each wearing a different one, and twelve full-screen effects.
Left and right switch the screen effect: sepia, duotone, night vision, thermal, chromatic aberration, underwater...
Back in the editor. Every effect is a node graph: this is the Duotone one, opened from the Scene Shaders list.
Let me give it more room...
...and press F to centre the whole graph: the scene texture goes through Grayscale, is mixed with two colours, and reaches the Output node.
Scripts open in the code editor, with syntax highlighting. This is the Lua script that drives this very demo.
It's a plain Lua file: the screen effects, the keys, and how each shader is switched on by its label.
Back to the default layout.
Now the objects. First, stop the scripts...
...and select an object that wears an object shader: Lava.
Its row in the Object Shaders panel expands to list the nodes and how they connect.
Edit nodes opens the object's own graph, live, in the same node editor.
F centres it: time and UV coordinates drive an offset, and the result is the lava texture, wired to a mesh instead of the screen.
More objects wear other node shaders: BurnDissolve...
Next object, next graph: DiagonalStripes.
Next object, next graph: FireGlow.
Next object, next graph: Hologram.
Next object, next graph: NeonPulse.
Next object, next graph: NormalColors.
Next object, next graph: HitFlash.
Click an object in the view, here the Lava sphere...
...and the docked inspector shows its transform, render settings, collider and more.
Drag a field and the object moves right there in the scene. Every change goes into the undo history.
Edit, Undo (Ctrl+Z) puts it back where it was. The history size is configurable.
And Redo (Ctrl+Y) brings the move back.
Play again, and on with the tour.
Thirty particle emitters on a carousel, starting with confetti. I'll flick through them backwards.
Black hole, fireworks, bubbles... every one is just a set of emitter parameters, no code.
Lightning, then a magic portal: a torus stood upright and swirling.
Particles can be born on a mesh surface, on a cone, a sphere or a ring.
And the newer spiral and vortex controls: a sprinkler, a galaxy with three arms, a tornado...
...and a helix. Thirty effects, all made of the same emitter.
The editor: every emitter on the carousel is a regular object you can select and tweak.
Thirty meshes flying as a swarm. They follow three simple rules: separation, alignment and cohesion.
The red cube is a predator: the boids steer away from it.
I can pause it, or make it faster.
The editor again: the swarm is a regular object, with its own inspector.
Three emitters each spawn a physics cube every half second. The wireframes are Bullet's own debug view.
You can see the real collision shapes, and the contact points where the cubes touch.
The engine keeps only the newest cubes, so the physics world stays light.
The launcher shoots bouncy physics projectiles at the base. A and D aim sideways, W and S up and down, with a smooth turn.
I nudge the aim and fire again: the shot arcs under gravity, hits the floor and bounces.
E adds power, so it flies further before the first bounce.
Now the physics debug view, with P: the wireframes are the real collision shapes Bullet is using.
A left click fires too.
P again hides it.
X makes the projectile bigger: more mass to push things around.
The editor, with the physics running underneath.
A first-person starter kit: a kinematic capsule with the camera in its eyes.
W and S walk forward and back; holding the left mouse button and dragging turns the head.
While it moves, the view sways gently from side to side, step after step, and A and D strafe.
Space jumps. It's a plain object script, so you can copy it onto your own character.
Third person: the camera follows from behind and always looks at the character.
Dragging the mouse turns the character, and the camera swings round with it.
Same idea: one object script, ready to reuse.
A 2D platformer inside a 3D level. No rigid bodies here: the player is moved by script.
Raycasts find the floor and the walls, which gives variable jump height, coyote time and jump buffering.
Up against a wall the player hooks on and slides down it. Space is a wall jump: it kicks off, D brings it back.
Jump after jump, it climbs the block and the wall.
And J attacks.
The editor around the 2D platformer.
A twin-stick shooter: one stick moves, the other aims. It works with a gamepad, or keyboard and mouse like now.
The mouse position becomes a world direction through a screen-to-world conversion.
R reloads, and the targets come back after a few seconds.
Last stop: the editor. Everything in it is a dockable window.
The Layouts menu rearranges the whole GUI. This one, Coding, puts the code editor in the middle.
Design gives the scene all the space it can get...
...and Default brings back the usual arrangement. F6, F7 and F8 do the same, holding Right Ctrl while the scripts run.
The Windows menu lists every window of the editor: scene objects, properties, project, files, logs, profiler...
Each one can be shown, hidden or docked wherever you like.
The menu bar holds the rest: script controls, add object, video, colliders, illumination, camera, sound, logs, layouts, interface...
Add Object creates any entity type of the engine: meshes, animated models, lights, particle emitters, sound sources...
And that's the tour. Every demo is a small, readable Lua script. Thanks for watching!
UI widgets are described in JSON files: a nested panel, a list, and single cards.
Lua only feeds them data every frame. The layout stays out of the code.
And here is the tool to edit them.
Windows, UI Manager: every widget loaded in the engine, in one list.
The icon at the window's top right isolates it: every other window closes and the scene stays in view.
I slide it to the right, so the widgets in the middle stay visible.
Type in the filter to narrow it down, and pick a widget.
A widget is a list of elements. Click one to see it.
The first one is a rect: the card's background.
Layout: where the element sits.
Identity and type: its id and what it is.
The type selector lists every kind of element: rect, image, text, bars...
Then an image: the avatar.
Text elements: the name...
...and the subtitle, filled in from Lua.
And a progress bar for the health.
Another widget: the nested panel, drawn from its JSON file.
Scale resizes the whole widget at once, with every element inside it.
Drag it back down and the widget shrinks again.
X % and Y % place it as a fraction of the window, so it fits any resolution.
Further down: background, frame, border and text settings.
The Frame section takes a 9-slice image: corners stay sharp and the edges stretch.
Window back in place...
...and the same icon brings the other windows back.
Back to the demo.
Every way of drawing text: TTF auto-sized, TTF with a fixed size, centred, aligned, cached...
The glyph atlas is the cheapest one, perfect for HUDs that change every frame.
The cursor changes with whatever is under the mouse. The engine tells the script which object is picked.
It's the same pattern the RTS uses.
I can also force a specific cursor with 1 to 4, and 0 goes back to automatic.
Selecting things RTS-style: a click selects one object, and Ctrl plus click adds more to the group.
The group has its own centre, and I can move all of it at once with W A S D.
R clears the selection.
A rectangle selection with Ctrl and drag picks several at once.
Positional sound: four looping sources in space. The camera is the listener, and volume falls off with distance.
The camera circles the sources, always looking at the centre: the volume of each one rises and falls as it gets closer.
The panel lists distance, volume and left/right pan of every source, and changes as the camera moves.
Keys 1 to 4 mute each source on its own.
P switches the left/right panning off and on.
TAB picks the source to tune.
X grows its inner radius: full volume now reaches farther.
Z shrinks it again.
V widens the outer radius: the sound now fades out over a longer distance.
And C narrows it. All of it live, with setInnerRadius and setOuterRadius.
Playing an MP4 from a script, full screen first.
Now the same video in a framed plane, with the scene visible around it.
And I can switch between both while it plays.
A stress test: spawn static meshes, physics bodies, lights, particles, animated meshes, in batches.
The FPS readout tells how far the engine can go on this machine.
There's a Profiler window in the editor to see where each frame goes.
And that's the tour. Thanks for watching!
